new_note: *And Jacob said to Joseph, Now I will die cheerfully after I have seen your face, that you are still living and with glory.* (Jasher 55:16). *And Yashar'el (Israel) said unto Joseph, Now let me die, since I have seen thy face, because thou art yet alive.* (Genesis 46:30). Jacob says the same thing in both books, and he says it for the same reason. The face he had mourned as dead is in front of him, alive and in glory, and there is nothing left for this life to give him. Genesis has him ready to die having seen it; Jasher has him die cheerfully. A father who has his son back has nothing more to ask.
member_note: Jasher 55:16 — *Now I will die cheerfully after I have seen your face.* Jacob's word on seeing Joseph alive, the same word Genesis 46:30 gives him.

new_note: *And Pharaoh said to Joseph, Place your father and brethren in the best part of the land, withhold not from them all that is good, and cause them to eat of the fat of the land.* (Jasher 55:22). *The land of Egypt is before thee; in the best of the land make thy father and brethren to dwell; in the land of Goshen let them dwell: and if thou knowest any men of activity among them, then make them rulers over my cattle.* (Genesis 47:6). Pharaoh's grant in Jasher is the decree Genesis records, and Joseph's answer in the next verse of Jasher names Goshen just as Pharaoh names it here. The best of the land is given to shepherds out of Canaan by the king of Egypt, and it is given because of Joseph. Yahuah (the Lord) had sent him ahead to keep the family alive, and now the family is settled on the fat of the land by the word of the very throne whose successors would enslave their children.
member_note: Jasher 55:22 — *Place your father and brethren in the best part of the land.* Pharaoh's grant, the same decree as Genesis 47:6.

new_note: *And Jacob said to Joseph and to his sons, Behold I die, and the Elohim (God) of your ancestors will visit you, and bring you back to the land, which Yahuah (the Lord) sware to give to you and to your children after you, now therefore when I am dead, bury me in the cave which is in Machpelah in Hebron in the land of Canaan, near my ancestors.* (Jasher 56:3). *And he charged them, and said unto them, I am to be gathered unto my people: bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,* (Genesis 49:29). The charge is the same charge. Jacob will not be buried in Egypt; he binds his sons to carry him to the cave at Machpelah where his fathers already lie. Jasher adds what the dying man says before the charge, that Elohim (God) will visit them and bring them back to the land Yahuah (the Lord) swore to give. The burial is the first step of that return, the father going home ahead of the children.
member_note: Jasher 56:3 — *bury me in the cave which is in Machpelah in Hebron.* Jacob's burial charge, with the promise that Elohim (God) will visit them and bring them back.

new_note: *And after that Yahudah (Judah) spake to Jacob, his father, and said to him: “Bend your bow, father, and send forth your arrows and cast down the adversary and slay the enemy; and may you have the power, for we shall not slay your brother, for he is such as you, and he is like you: let us give him (this) honour.”* (Jubilees 38:1). *Only teach your sons the bow and all the weapons of war, in order that they may fight the battles of their brother who will rule over his enemies.* (Jasher 56:9). In both books it is Yahudah (Judah) and the bow. Jubilees puts the bow in Jacob's own hand at Yahudah's (Judah's) urging while Jacob still lives, and names the enemy as Esau; Jasher puts the same charge on Jacob's deathbed, Yahudah (Judah) to teach his sons the bow and every weapon of war so that they can fight the battles of the brother who rules over his enemies, and the enemy who comes against that house before the chapter ends is Esau. Two tellings of one memory, that the tribe that reigns is the tribe taught to fight.
member_note: Jasher 56:9 — *Only teach your sons the bow and all the weapons of war.* Jacob's deathbed charge to Yahudah (Judah), the bow against Esau's house that Jubilees 38:1 also remembers.
flag: The two books set the war with Esau at different times (Jubilees while Jacob lives, Jasher after his death); the note keeps the shared memory of Yahudah and the bow without asserting which tradition stands behind the other, as the old note did.

new_note: *And it shall come to pass when you shall go after Elohim to serve him and will teach your children after you, and your children’s children, to know Yahuah (the Lord), then will Yahuah (the Lord) raise up to you and your children a servant from amongst your children, and Yahuah (the Lord) will deliver you through his hand from all affliction, and bring you out of Egypt and bring you back to the land of your fathers to inherit it securely.* (Jasher 56:21). *By faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Yashar'el (Israel); and gave commandment concerning his bones.* (Hebrews 11:22). Jacob dies foreseeing the bringing out of Egypt; Joseph dies foreseeing the same departing and gives commandment about his bones because of it. Hebrews counts Joseph's word as faith, and Jasher shows where the son heard it first: at his father's bed, hearing that Yahuah (the Lord) would raise up a servant from among their children and bring them back to the land of their fathers. Neither man saw it. Both died holding it.
member_note: Jasher 56:21 — *bring you out of Egypt and bring you back to the land of your fathers.* Jacob foresees the departing Joseph will foretell over his bones in Hebrews 11:22.

new_note: *And all the souls that went forth from the loins of Jacob, were seventy souls; these are they who came with Jacob their father to Egypt to dwell there: and Joseph and all his brethren dwelt securely in Egypt, and they ate of the best of Egypt all the days of the life of Joseph.* (Jasher 59:19). *And all the souls that came out of the loins of Jacob were seventy souls: for Joseph was in Egypt already.* (Exodus 1:5). Jasher closes its roll of the family with the same seventy souls Exodus opens with, counted the same way, from the loins of Jacob. The number is the seed of promise as it stood going down into Egypt, a household small enough to name one by one. Exodus turns the page and says they multiplied until the land was filled with them; Jasher ends the sentence with them eating of the best of Egypt all the days of Joseph. Both books want the reader to see how few they were before they became a people.
member_note: Jasher 59:19 — *all the souls that went forth from the loins of Jacob, were seventy souls.* The seventy Exodus 1:5 counts, the household as it stood going down into Egypt.

new_note: *And this was also from Yahuah (the Lord), for the children of Israel, to benefit them in their latter days, in order that all the children of Israel might know Yahuah their Elohim (the Lord their God).* (Jasher 63:7). *But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but Elohim (God) meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.* (Genesis 50:20). Joseph said it of his brothers' betrayal, that they meant evil and Elohim (God) meant good; Jasher says the same of the bondage itself. The Egyptians embittered the lives of the sons of Jacob out of ingratitude, having forgotten who fed them in the famine, and yet Jasher names the affliction as being from Yahuah (the Lord), set for the good of the children of Yashar'el (Israel) in their latter days. The purpose was that they would know him. Hard labor under a king who did not know Joseph was the ground in which a people learned the name of the Elohim (God) of their fathers.
member_note: Jasher 63:7 — *to benefit them in their latter days.* The bondage itself named as from Yahuah (the Lord) and for their good, as Joseph said of his brothers' evil.

new_note: *And when they were departed, behold, the angel of Yahuah (Lord) appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.* (Matthew 2:13). *There was a man in the land of Egypt of the seed of Levi, whose name was Amram, the son of Kehath, the son of Levi, the son of Israel.* (Jasher 67:1). Jasher 67 opens where the story of the deliverer begins, with his father, a man of the seed of Levi living in Egypt in the years when Pharaoh would begin to spill the blood of the male children. Matthew 2 opens the story of the greater deliverer the same way, with a father warned by the angel of Yahuah (the Lord) to carry the child into Egypt because a king is seeking to destroy him. Moses was hidden in Egypt from Pharaoh; Yahusha (Jesus) was hidden in Egypt from Herod. The kingdom of man always moves to kill the promised seed at its birth, and there is always a household ready to hide the child.
member_note: Jasher 67:1 — *There was a man in the land of Egypt of the seed of Levi.* The deliverer's story opens with his father in Egypt, as Matthew 2:13 opens with Joseph carrying the child there.

new_note: *Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men.* (Matthew 2:16). *And the woman conceived and bare a daughter, and she called her name Miriam, because in those days the Egyptians had embittered the lives of the children of Israel.* (Jasher 67:3). Jasher tells the Egyptian slaughter in fuller detail than Exodus 1 gives it, and it counts from inside one family: Miriam is named for the bitterness of the days she was born into, and in the next verse Aaron is born as Pharaoh begins to spill the blood of the male children of Yashar'el (Israel). Herod at Bethlehem is the same hand in a later century, a king killing the infants of a town to reach one child. The kingdom of man always moves to kill the promised seed at its birth. It failed with Moses and it failed with Yahusha (Jesus).
member_note: Jasher 67:3 — *the Egyptians had embittered the lives of the children of Israel.* Miriam named for the bitter days; Herod's Bethlehem is the same hand in a later century.

new_note: *Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men.* (Matthew 2:16). *And she conceived again and bare a son and she called his name Aaron, for in the days of her conception, Pharaoh began to spill the blood of the male children of Israel.* (Jasher 67:4). Jasher gives the decree a date: it began in the days Aaron was conceived, and the boy's own name carries it. Matthew gives Herod's decree a date too, from two years old and under, reckoned from the time the wise men told him. Pharaoh spilled the blood of the male children of Yashar'el (Israel) to keep a deliverer from rising; Herod slew the children of Bethlehem to keep the King from rising. Same fear, same answer, and in both cases the king's sword missed the one child it was sharpened for.
member_note: Jasher 67:4 — *Pharaoh began to spill the blood of the male children of Israel.* The decree dated by Aaron's conception; Herod's decree at Bethlehem is the same move against the promised seed.

new_note: *And the children of Esau sent to Pethor, which is upon the river, and they fetched from there a young man of beautiful eyes and comely aspect, whose name was Saul, and they made him king over them in the place of Samlah.* (Jasher 69:2). *And Samlah died, and Saul of Rehoboth by the river reigned in his stead.* (Genesis 36:37). The Torah's list of the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over the children of Yashar'el (Israel) names the same Saul, from a city upon the river, succeeding the same Samlah. Genesis calls his city Rehoboth; Jasher calls it Pethor, and tells how the children of Esau went and fetched him, a young man chosen for his looks, and made him king. The two books agree on the man, the order, and the river, and Jasher supplies how he came to the throne.
member_note: Jasher 69:2 — *they made him king over them in the place of Samlah.* The Saul of Genesis 36:37, from a city upon the river, and how the children of Esau fetched him.

new_note: *So Moses went forth from the land of Cush, and went home and ceased to reign over Cush, and Moses was sixty-six years old when he went out of the land of Cush, for the thing was from Yahuah (the Lord), for the period had arrived which he had appointed in the days of old, to bring forth Israel from the affliction of the children of Ham.* (Jasher 76:12). *Then fled Moses at this saying, and was a stranger in the land of Madian, where he begat two sons.* (Acts 7:29). Stephen moves Moses from the flight out of Egypt straight to Midian; Jasher fills the years between with a reign over Cush that ends only when Moses is sixty-six and the appointed period has come. Both agree on the shape of the thing: a long stretch away from his brethren, a stranger, before the call. Jasher says why the Cush years end when they do, because the thing was from Yahuah (the Lord), who had fixed the time in the days of old to bring Yashar'el (Israel) out from the affliction of the children of Ham. The deliverer's waiting was on a schedule he did not set.
member_note: Jasher 76:12 — *the period had arrived which he had appointed in the days of old.* The Cush years end on Yahuah's (the Lord's) schedule, the long stretch away from his brethren that Stephen names in Acts 7:29.

new_note: *And Zipporah conceived and bare a son and he called his name Gershom, for he said, I was a stranger in a foreign land; but he circumcised not his foreskin, at the command of Reuel his father-in-law.* (Jasher 78:9). *And she bare him a son, and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land.* (Exodus 2:22). The naming of Gershom is the same in both books, nearly word for word: a stranger in a foreign land. Jasher adds something Exodus does not say here, that the boy was not circumcised, and gives the reason, Reuel's command to the son-in-law living under his roof. The next verse of Jasher has the second son circumcised and named for deliverance, so the two births mark the two halves of Moses' time in Midian, the stranger first and then the man Elohim (God) had helped.
member_note: Jasher 78:9 — *he called his name Gershom, for he said, I was a stranger in a foreign land.* The naming Exodus 2:22 records, with Jasher adding that the boy was left uncircumcised at Reuel's command.

new_note: *And she conceived again and bare a son, but circumcised his foreskin, and called his name Eliezer, for Moses said, Because the Elohim (God) of my fathers was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.* (Jasher 78:10). *This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did Elohim (God) send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush.* (Acts 7:35). Eliezer's name is Moses' own confession that the Elohim (God) of his fathers was his help and delivered him from the sword of Pharaoh. Stephen says the same of him from the other side: the man his brethren refused is the one Elohim (God) sent back as ruler and deliverer. The one delivered becomes the deliverer. Jasher has Moses name the rescue over his son in Midian, years before the bush, and Acts has the rescue become the sending.
member_note: Jasher 78:10 — *the Elohim (God) of my fathers was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.* Eliezer's name confesses the rescue; Acts 7:35 has the rescued man sent back as deliverer.

new_note: *And Yahuah (the Lord) sent by the hand of Aaron and turned all the waters of Egypt into blood, with all their streams and rivers.* (Jasher 80:3). *And Yahuah (LORD) spake unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Take thy rod, and stretch out thine hand upon the waters of Egypt, upon their streams, upon their rivers, and upon their ponds, and upon all their pools of water, that they may become blood; and that there may be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood, and in vessels of stone.* (Exodus 7:19). Jasher gives the first plague in one line and Exodus gives the command behind it, but both put the hand on Aaron. Yahuah (the Lord) sends by Aaron's hand, Aaron stretches out the rod, and every stream and river of Egypt turns to blood. Jasher's next verses follow the plague into the pitcher and the cup, which is what Exodus means by vessels of wood and vessels of stone. The plagues begin where Egypt drinks.
member_note: Jasher 80:3 — *turned all the waters of Egypt into blood, with all their streams and rivers.* The first plague by Aaron's hand, as Exodus 7:19 commands it.

new_note: *And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians, and there was a great cry throughout Egypt in that night, for there was not a house in which there was not a corpse.* (Jasher 80:44). *And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he, and all his servants, and all the Egyptians; and there was a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead.* (Exodus 12:30). Jasher 80:44 is Exodus 12:30 nearly word for word: the king rising in the night, the servants, all the Egyptians, the cry, and not a house without its dead. Jasher adds in the next verse that even the carved likenesses of the firstborn fell from the walls, so that the judgment reached the images as well as the sons. The night Yahuah (the Lord) passed through Egypt is told in both books with the same breath.
member_note: Jasher 80:44 — *there was not a house in which there was not a corpse.* The night of the firstborn, Exodus 12:30 nearly word for word.

new_note: *Also a mixed multitude went up with them, and flocks and herds, even much cattle.* (Jasher 81:2). *And Yahuah (LORD) gave the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they lent unto them such things as they required. And they spoiled the Egyptians.* (Exodus 12:36). Jasher counts what went up out of Egypt with the children of Yashar'el (Israel): a mixed multitude, flocks and herds, much cattle. Exodus 12:36 adds what they carried, the things the Egyptians lent them when Yahuah (the Lord) gave the people favour in their sight. Together the two verses show a people leaving not as fugitives but as a nation going out with its wealth and its herds after the years of hard labor. The spoiling of Egypt and the cattle of Jasher are the same going out seen from two sides.
member_note: Jasher 81:2 — *Also a mixed multitude went up with them, and flocks and herds, even much cattle.* What went up out of Egypt, beside the goods Exodus 12:36 says the Egyptians lent them.
flag: Exodus 12:38 (the mixed multitude and the very much cattle) is the closer canon line to Jasher 81:2 than 12:36; the card is kept on 12:36 as given and the note joins the two as one going out.

new_note: *And Moses said to them, Fear not, stand still and see the salvation of Yahuah (the Lord) which He will effect this day for you.* (Jasher 81:28). *And Moses said unto the people, Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of Yahuah (LORD), which he will shew to you to day: for the Egyptians whom ye have seen to day, ye shall see them again no more for ever.* (Exodus 14:13). Moses' word at the sea is the same in both books: fear not, stand still, see the salvation of Yahuah (the Lord) which he will work this day. Jasher tells us whom he was answering. The people had broken into divisions, one resolved to throw itself into the sea, another to go back to Egypt, and the charge to stand still is spoken into that panic. Exodus adds the promise that the Egyptians they saw that day they would never see again.
member_note: Jasher 81:28 — *Fear not, stand still and see the salvation of Yahuah (the Lord).* Moses' word at the sea, Exodus 14:13 spoken into a people split into divisions.

new_note: *And Moses said to Joshua, Be strong and courageous, for you will make the children of Israel inherit the land, and Yahuah (the Lord) will be with you, he will not leave you nor forsake you, be not afraid nor disheartened.* (Jasher 87:4). *Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.* (Hebrews 13:5). Moses gives Joshua the promise as he hands him the people: Yahuah (the Lord) will be with you, he will not leave you nor forsake you. Hebrews quotes that same promise to its readers as a thing he has said, and builds contentment on it. The word spoken at the edge of the land to the man who would lead Yashar'el (Israel) into it is the word still standing for the scattered children centuries later. Nothing between Moses and Hebrews withdrew it. It is the same mouth and the same promise.
member_note: Jasher 87:4 — *he will not leave you nor forsake you.* The promise to Joshua that Hebrews 13:5 still quotes as his word.

new_note: *Now therefore observe all the words of this law, and walk in the way of Yahuah your Elohim, turn not from the way which Yahuah (the Lord) has commanded you, either to the right or to the left.* (Jasher 87:6). *Ye shall observe to do therefore as Yahuah Elohaychem (the LORD your God) hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.* (Deuteronomy 5:32). Jasher has Moses closing his life with the charge Deuteronomy records: observe all the words of this law, walk in the way Yahuah (the Lord) commanded, turn not to the right or the left. The two verses are the same instruction, and in both it comes with the whole law attached, not a part of it. The way is the commandments. To turn aside from them in either direction, adding or subtracting, is to leave the way, and that is the thing Moses forbids with his last words.
member_note: Jasher 87:6 — *observe all the words of this law, and walk in the way of Yahuah your Elohim.* Moses' last charge, the Deuteronomy 5:32 word to keep the whole law and turn neither right nor left.

new_note: *And Moses finished commanding the children of Israel, and Yahuah (the Lord) said to him, saying, Go up to the Mount Abarim and die there, and be gathered to your people as Aaron your brother was gathered.* (Jasher 87:9). *And die in the mount whither thou goest up, and be gathered unto thy people; as Aaron thy brother died in mount Hor, and was gathered unto his people:* (Deuteronomy 32:50). Yahuah (the Lord) sends Moses up the mountain with the same words in both books: die there, be gathered to your people, as Aaron your brother was gathered. Jasher compresses the Torah's longer speech into one sentence and keeps its shape. The man who led Yashar'el (Israel) out does not lead them in; he goes the way his brother went, and the people he leaves have just been given the whole law to walk by.
member_note: Jasher 87:9 — *be gathered to your people as Aaron your brother was gathered.* The call to Abarim, Deuteronomy 32:50 in Jasher's wording.

new_note: *Rise up and pass the Jordan to the land which I have given to the children of Israel, and you shall make the children of Israel inherit the land.* (Jasher 88:2). *Moses my servant is dead; now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, thou, and all this people, unto the land which I do give to them, even to the children of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Joshua 1:2). The command to Joshua is the same command. Moses is dead, the people are on the east bank, and Yahuah (the Lord) tells the new leader to rise, cross the Jordan, and bring the children of Yashar'el (Israel) into the land already given. Jasher adds the charge that Joshua will make them inherit it, the very thing Moses had told him in Jasher 87:4. The gift was spoken before the crossing; the crossing is the people walking into what was already theirs.
member_note: Jasher 88:2 — *Rise up and pass the Jordan to the land which I have given.* The commission of Joshua 1:2, with the charge to make the children inherit it.

new_note: *Every place upon which the sole of your feet shall tread shall belong to you, from the wilderness of Lebanon to the great river the river of Perath shall be your boundary.* (Jasher 88:3). *Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread shall be yours: from the wilderness and Lebanon, from the river, the river Euphrates, even unto the uttermost sea shall your coast be.* (Deuteronomy 11:24). The boundary Yahuah (the Lord) gives Joshua is the boundary Moses had already announced in Deuteronomy: every place the sole of the foot treads, from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great river. Jasher calls that river by its Hebrew name, Perath, which is the Euphrates. The word to Joshua repeats the word through Moses because the land was promised before either of them, sworn to the fathers, and each generation hears the same borders read back to it.
member_note: Jasher 88:3 — *Every place upon which the sole of your feet shall tread shall belong to you.* The borders Moses had already read out in Deuteronomy 11:24, Perath being the Euphrates.

new_note: *And the people went up from Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped in Gilgal at the eastern corner of Jericho.* (Jasher 88:10). *And the people came up out of Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and encamped in Gilgal, in the east border of Jericho.* (Joshua 4:19). Jasher and Joshua agree to the day and the place: the tenth day of the first month, the camp at Gilgal on the east side of Jericho. The tenth of the first month is the day the Torah sets for taking the Passover lamb, and the next verse of Jasher has them keeping the Passover at Gilgal on the fourteenth as it is written in the law of Moses. The people enter the land on the lamb's day and keep the feast four days later, forty years after the first Passover in Egypt.
member_note: Jasher 88:10 — *on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped in Gilgal.* The day and place of Joshua 4:19, the lamb's day, with Passover kept four days on.

new_note: *These are the inheritances which Elazer the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers of the tribes portioned out to the children of Israel by lot in Shiloh, before Yahuah (the Lord), at the door of the tabernacle, and they left off dividing the land.* (Jasher 90:23). *And these are the countries which the children of Yashar'el (Israel) inherited in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers of the tribes of the children of Yashar'el (Israel), distributed for inheritance to them.* (Joshua 14:1). The same three parties divide the land in both books: Eleazar the priest, Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers of the tribes, and they do it by lot. Jasher sets the scene more closely, at Shiloh, before Yahuah (the Lord), at the door of the tabernacle, so that the inheritance of every tribe is portioned out in his presence rather than by the strength of any man's hand. Joshua 14:1 is the heading of the record; Jasher 90:23 is its close.
member_note: Jasher 90:23 — *portioned out to the children of Israel by lot in Shiloh.* The division Joshua 14:1 heads, done before Yahuah (the Lord) at the tabernacle door.
flag: Live Jasher text spells the priest "Elazer" where Joshua has "Eleazar"; quoted as it stands, in case the author wants the Jasher spelling normalized.

new_note: *And Yahuah (the Lord) gave the land to the Israelites, and they possessed it as Yahuah (the Lord) had spoken to them, and as Yahuah (the Lord) had sworn to their ancestors.* (Jasher 90:24). *And Yahuah (LORD) gave unto Yashar'el (Israel) all the land which he sware to give unto their fathers; and they possessed it, and dwelt therein.* (Joshua 21:43). Both books close the conquest with the same sentence: Yahuah (the Lord) gave the land, as he had sworn to the fathers, and Yashar'el (Israel) possessed it. Jasher's next verse goes on as Joshua 21 does, rest from every enemy and not one word failing of all the good he had spoken. The giving is his; the possessing is theirs; and the oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is the reason for both.
member_note: Jasher 90:24 — *they possessed it as Yahuah (the Lord) had spoken to them.* The close of the conquest as Joshua 21:43 gives it, the land given as sworn to the fathers.
